title: Enlarged Lawson-Haggart band and its free recording style
summary: Lawson and Haggart augment the band with Butterfield, Hucko, Bud Freeman and Lou McGarity, give everyone freedom, and keep a first sight-read take of 'Tiger Rag'.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: And I need an insertion here. That was the Bicentennial that we were playing -- I left out the word 'bi', which was of course, nationwide -- rather, our nation's great celebration. I noticed that in playing this back, that I had talked into this machine, this fool machine here for 10 or 15 minutes about the Lawson-Haggard band, and upon our recording with a larger group, and I forgot to push all the proper buttons. So it was deleted. However, Bob Haggard and Lawson in doing the arrangements, wanted to enlarge upon the band, certain things that Decca picked for us to do, they wanted a bigger sound -- we augmented the band, so we had two Lawson-Haggard bands. We had the original which I mentioned, and then some dates he would add Billy Butterfield on trumpet and Peanut Hucko on clarinet or tenor, and he used Bud Freeman on tenor, and the most wonderful, one of my greatest musical loves in life, Lou McGerrity on trombone.
And of course we added George Burns, who was working at that time on the Hit Parade. So I hope this might be inserted -- it's of importance to me.
I went through great detail, and that was left out, the freedom that Bob Haggard and Yank gave us -- he said to

just go ahead and play and if you want anything, let us know, if you want to change anything, let us know, if you want to go back and redo the thing, it was just a happy relationship, everybody must be pleased, or we wouldn't continue.

We made things with -- so fast, that were excellent, there was very little going over the tapes. I don't think I go to where tapes were coming in then. Instead of tapes, and it was easy to insert, it was becoming easy to insert, or we'd do introductions and endings without doing the whole thing over again. But we didn't do too much of that. I remember we brought in an arrangement of 'Tiger Rag' in a modern vein, and we ran it down once -- this was by sight -- everybody happened to be not only a jazz artist, but a schooled musician in that group. And we ran it down once, and said well, now we'll try it out. We just sight read it.

Well, we tried a couple of times, and the tapes kind of fouled up, and Yank said, 'Let me hear that first one'. And we played back the first tape, and that's the one they took. Now this is a phenomenon in reading something down and have it swing, and the jazz solo, of course, is another thing, too, but everything was just a beautiful, swinging feeling, and so they took the first tape. And I just mention this as an -- such an unusual organization in its field.

Bob Haggart told me to play any way you want to, if it's too loud, we'll call it down in the control room, do whatever you want, just use your own feeling and your own taste -- then he told me what to do. Now, it's seldom in this world, unless you're the leader and you're the drummer, like Buddy Rich -- and there are only one or two of those around, possibly Louie Belson, that anybody that has the opportunity to work with their own natural feeling without somebody standing over them with a baseball bat.
I can still Yank Lawson's voice saying; 'be happy, Cliff, do whatever you want.'1)
